'''Yatsushiro Shrine''' (やつしろじんじゃ), also known as '''Myōken Shrine''' (みょうけんぐう) or '''Myōken-san,''' is a [[Shinto]] shrine located in [[Yatsushiro City]], {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|qid=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, Japan. Historically Ranked as a prefectural shrine under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|State Shinto system]], it comprises three main shrines: the Upper Shrine, the Middle Shrine, and the Lower Shrine, with the Lower Shrine currently serving as the main sanctuary. Yatsushiro Shrine is counted among the "Three Great Myōken Shrines" of Japan alongside [[Sōma Nakamura Shrine]] in {{ill|Fukushima Prefecture|en|Fukushima Prefecture|qid=Q71707|lt=Fukushima Prefecture}} and {{ill|Nose Myōkenzan|fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nose Myōkenzan|qq=}} in {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|qid=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}}.

== History ==
According to the ''Myōken Shrine Chronicle'' written in 1730 (Kyōhō 15), the shrine was first established as the Upper Shrine atop Mount Yokodake in 795 CE (Enryaku 14).<ref name="Hayase">{{Cite journal|和書|author=Hayase Terumi|title=囃されない笠鉾：八代妙見祭の笠鉾について|journal=造り物の文化史|date=2014|publisher=勉誠出版|isbn=9784585230281|qq=draft}}</ref> The Middle Shrine was constructed in 1160 CE (Eiryaku 1), and the Lower Shrine was built in 1186 CE (Bunji 2) under the imperial command of {{ill|Emperor Go-Toba|en|Emperor Go-Toba|qid=Q316658|lt=Emperor Go-Toba}}, with construction overseen by Kengyō Sanmi, Ōe no Ason Takafusa.<ref>Suzuki Kyō, ed. ''Kumamoto no Jinja to Tera.'' Kumamoto Nichinichi Shinbunsha, 1980, p. 90.</ref>

Until 1870 (Meiji 3), the shrine was known as Myōken Shrine. The deity {{ill|Myōken|en|Myōken|qid=Q10960623|lt=Myōken}} symbolizes the [[:en:Pole Star|Pole Star]] and the {{ill|Big Dipper|en|Big Dipper|qid=Q10460|lt=Big Dipper}}. The shrine functioned as a joint Shinto-Buddhist temple complex and was widely revered as the principal shrine (Ichinomiya) of the three districts of Yatsushiro, Shimo-Mashiki, and Ashikita. Following the [[Shinbutsu bunri]] (separation of Shinto and Buddhism) policies of the Meiji era, the shrine was renamed Yatsushiro Shrine, with [[Ame-no-Minakanushi|Ame-no-Minakanushi]] and [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kunino-Tokotachi-no-Kami]] enshrined as its primary deities.<ref>Kumamoto Nichinichi Shinbun, ed. ''Kumamoto Prefecture Encyclopedia.'' Kumamoto Nichinichi Shinbunsha, 1982, p. 456.</ref>

The annual ''Myōken Festival,'' held on {{ill|November 22|en|November 22|qid=Q3025|lt=November 22}}–{{ill|November 23|en|November 23|qid=Q3021|lt=November 23}}, is one of the '''Three Great Festivals of Kyūshū''' and has been designated as an [[:en:Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property]] by the Japanese government.<ref>From the historical records of Yatsushiro Shrine.</ref>

== Enshrined Deities ==
* [[Ame-no-Minakanushi|Ame-no-Minakanushi]] (天之御中主神)
* [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kunino-Tokotachi-no-Kami]] (国常立尊)

== Myōken Festival ==
=== Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property (National Designation) ===
The '''Myōken Festival''' (やつしろ みょうけんさい), held annually in the autumn, is among the '''Three Great Festivals of Kyūshū''', alongside the {{ill|Nagasaki Kunchi|en|Nagasaki Kunchi|qid=Q114712|lt=Nagasaki Kunchi}} of {{ill|Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)|en|Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)|qid=Q84028|lt=Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)}} and the {{ill|Life release|en|Life release|qid=Q11078912|lt=Hōjō-e}} of {{ill|Hakozaki Shrine|en|Hakozaki Shrine|qid=Q714742|lt=Hakozaki Shrine}}.<ref>The "Three Great Festivals of Kyūshū" sometimes include {{ill|Hakata Gion Yamakasa|en|Hakata Gion Yamakasa|qid=Q1749262|lt=Hakata Gion Yamakasa}} instead of the Hakozaki Shrine's Hōjō-e.</ref> The festival features a procession of floats and other ceremonial objects, some of which date back to the late Edo period. It was registered as part of UNESCO's [[:en:Intangible Cultural Heritage|Intangible Cultural Heritage]] in {{ill|2016|en|2016|qid=Q25245|lt=2016}} under the broader category of ''[[Yama, Hoko, Yatai, float festivals in Japan|Mountain, Float, and Procession Festivals]].''<ref>{{Cite web|和書|title=八代妙見祭の神幸行事とは?|url=http://www.city.yatsushiro.lg.jp/bunka/kiji0031289/index.html|accessdate=2024-01-12}}</ref>

The festival includes:
* ''Oshimochi'' (Procession Downward) on {{ill|November 22|en|November 22|qid=Q3025|lt=November 22}}
* ''Onobori'' (Procession Upward) on {{ill|November 23|en|November 23|qid=Q3021|lt=November 23}}

== Himuro Festival ==
The '''Himuro Festival''' (ひむろまつり) is held annually from {{ill|May 31|en|May 31|qid=Q2591|lt=May 31}} to {{ill|June 1|en|June 1|qid=Q2625|lt=June 1}} at Yatsushiro Shrine. It is rooted in the early Edo period, when Yatsushiro Castle lord {{ill|Hosokawa Tadaoki|en|Hosokawa Tadaoki|qid=Q1147154|lt=Hosokawa Tadaoki}} offered snow stored in the ice house of Mount Miroomiya to pray for good health.<ref>{{Cite web|和書|title=妙見さんの氷室祭り|url=http://www.pref.kumamoto.jp/site/arinomama/myouhimuro.html|accessdate=2014-02-12}}</ref>

== Main Shrine Festivals ==
* Rice Planting Ceremony ({{ill|January 3|en|January 3|qid=Q2156|lt=January 3}})
* Seventeenth Night Festival ({{ill|July 17|en|July 17|qid=Q2729|lt=July 17}})

== Associated Shrines ==
=== Reifu Shrine ===
* '''Deities''': Pole Star, Reifu Sonsei
* '''Significance''': Reifu Shrine is an auxiliary shrine of Yatsushiro Shrine, revered as the head shrine of the deity {{ill|Chintaku Reifu|ja|鎮宅霊符神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinchō Reifu Shin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鎮宅霊符|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q86740326}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established during the reign of {{ill|Empress Suiko|en|Empress Suiko|qid=Q298057|lt=Empress Suiko}} by Prince [[Rinshō Taishi]] of [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]]. It is believed to bring prosperity and avert misfortune.<ref>Kumamoto Educational Association, ed. ''Yatsushiro District Chronicle,'' 1927, p. 396.</ref>

'''Yatsushiro Shrine''' (やつしろじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Yatsushiro|en|Yatsushiro|qid=Q734479|lt=Yatsushiro}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|qid=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}. Commonly known as '''Myōken-gū''' (妙見宮) or '''Myōken-san''', it was historically Ranked as a prefectural shrine under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|qid=Q712534|lt=Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines}}. The shrine comprises three precincts: the U11er Shrine (Kamimiya), Middle Shrine (Nakamiya), and Lower Shrine (Shimomiya). Currently, the Lower Shrine serves as the main shrine. Alongside {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|ja|相馬妙見|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sōma Myōken|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天之御中主神|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2842779}} in Fukushima Prefecture and {{ill|Myōkenzan (Osaka and Hyōgo)|lt=Nose Myōken|ja|妙見山 (能勢)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōkenzan (Osaka and Hyōgo)|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 妙見山 (大阪府・兵庫県)}} in Osaka Prefecture, it is considered one of the "Three Great Myōken Shrines of Japan."

== History ==
According to the *Myōken-gū Jikki* (1730), the shrine was founded in 795 (Enryaku 14) at the summit of Yokodake, where the U11er Shrine was established. The Middle Shrine was built in 1160 (Eiryaku 1), and the Lower Shrine was constructed in 1186 (Bunji 2) as an imperial prayer offering by Emperor Go-Toba, under the direction of Lord Ōe Takafusa.<ref>Takashi Suzuki (ed.), *Kumamoto no Jinja to Tera*, Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbunsha, 1980, p. 90.</ref>

Until 1870 (Meiji 3), the shrine was known as Myōken-gū. The deity {{ill|Myōken|ja|妙見|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōken|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 妙見菩薩|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10960623}} symbolizes the North Star and the Big Di11er. As a dual Shinto-Buddhist shrine and temple, it garnered widespread reverence and thrived as the Ichinomiya of Yatsushiro, Shimo-Mashiki, and Ashikita Districts. In 1871 (Meiji 4), due to the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離令|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto-Buddhist separation|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to QID FIXED|qid=Q1970535|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1970535}}, the enshrined deities were identified as {{ill|Ame-no-Minakanushi|en|Ame-no-Minakanushi|qid=Q2842779|lt=Ame-no-Minakanushi}} and {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|en|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|qid=Q478504|lt=Kuni-no-Tokotachi}}, and the shrine was renamed Yatsushiro Shrine, attaining prefectural shrine status.<ref>*Kumamoto Prefectural Encyclopedia*, Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbunsha, 1982, p. 456.</ref>

The shrine’s annual *Myōken Festival*, held on November 22–23, is recognized as one of the *Three Great Festivals of Kyushu* and designated as a National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property.<ref>From Yatsushiro Shrine historical records.</ref>

* {{ill|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|en|Kuni-no-Tokotachi|qid=Q478504|lt=Kuni-no-Tokotachi}}

== Yatsushiro Myōken Festival ==
=== National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property ===
The *Yatsushiro Myōken Festival* (八代妙見祭) is the shrine’s autumn grand festival and one of Kyushu’s Three Great Festivals.<ref>The Three Great Festivals of Kyushu are the {{ill|Nagasaki Kunchi|en|Nagasaki Kunchi|qid=Q114712|lt=Nagasaki Kunchi}} of {{ill|Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)|en|Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)|qid=Q84028|lt=Suwa Shrine (Nagasaki)}}, the {{ill|Life release|en|Life release|qid=Q11078912|lt=Hōjō-e}} of {{ill|Hakozaki Shrine|en|Hakozaki Shrine|qid=Q714742|lt=Hakozaki Shrine}} in Fukuoka, and the Yatsushiro Myōken Festival. In some cases, {{ill|Hakata Gion Yamakasa|en|Hakata Gion Yamakasa|qid=Q1749262|lt=Hakata Gion Yamakasa}} replaces Hōjō-e.</ref> Designated a National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 2011 (Heisei 23), it was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016 as part of the "Yama, Hoko, and Yatai Festivals."

The festival is the largest ritual in the Yatsushiro area, with records of its observance dating back to 1515 (Eishō 12) in the *Yatsushiro Nikki*. Historically, the procession carried the deity between the Lower and Middle Shrines. After a decline during the Azuchi-Momoyama period, it was revived under the patronage of the Kato clan and later the Hosokawa and Matsui clans.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.city.yatsushiro.lg.jp/bunka/kiji0031289/index.html |title=About the Yatsushiro Myōken Festival (Yatsushiro City Official Website) |accessdate=2016-04-22}}</ref>

The festival features various traditional floats, including umbrellas, *kasaboko*, dragon and lion effigies, and a tortoise-serpent float inspired by the myth of {{ill|Black Turtle-Snake|en|Black Turtle-Snake|qid=Q125696|lt=Genbu}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.city.yatsushiro.lg.jp/bunka/kiji003312/index.html |title=Myōken Festival Materials (Yatsushiro City Official Website) |accessdate=2016-04-22}}</ref>

* November 22: *Oshitauri* (Descent)
* November 23: *Oagari* (Ascent)

== Himuro Festival ==
The *Himuro Festival* (氷室祭) is held annually from May 31 to June 1 to pray for good health and prosperity. It originates from a 17th-century tradition of offering snow stored in the local *himuro* (ice chamber) to the shrine by Yatsushiro Castle lord {{ill|Hosokawa Tadaoki|en|Hosokawa Tadaoki|qid=Q1147154|lt=Hosokawa Tadaoki}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pref.kumamoto.jp/site/arinomama/myouhimuro.html |title=Myōken-san Himuro Festival (Kumamoto Prefecture Website) |accessdate=2014-02-12}}</ref>

* '''17th Night Festival''' (July 17)

=== Reifu Shrine ===
* '''Enshrined Deities''': North Star, Reifu deity
* '''History''': Reifu Shrine (れいふじんじゃ) is a subordinate shrine of Yatsushiro Shrine and the principal shrine of {{ill|Chintaku Reifu|ja|鎮宅霊符神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chintaku Reifu Shin|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鎮宅霊符|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q86740326}}. According to tradition, the deity was introduced to Japan by {{ill|Prince Imseong|en|Prince Imseong|qid=Q716548|lt=Prince Imseong}}, the third prince of {{ill|Seong of Baekje|en|Seong of Baekje|qid=Q497911|lt=Seong of Baekje}}, and enshrined at Myōken-gū. While the shrine deteriorated during the {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|qid=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku}}, it was restored during the Taishō period.<ref>*Yatsushiro District Records*, Kumamoto Prefectural Education Association, 1927.</ref>
* '''location''': Approximately200 meters east of Yatsushiro Shrine.
